lessons.title: A five-step audit of your organisation's AI systems
lessons.subtitle: From existing records to a prioritised gap list

sections.title: Five steps for a defensible initial inventory
sections.content:
How long the inventory takes depends on the organisation, the number of systems, shadow IT, supplier records and the risk profile; there is no fixed time budget.

**1. Build the inventory.** The record of processing activities under Article 30 GDPR shows AI-supported processing of personal data. Systems without personal data and shadow AI turn up through IT asset and SaaS registers, procurement, supplier contracts, billing, browser or SSO approvals and interviews.

**2. Establish purpose and system boundary.** Write down which function actually runs; a product name says neither whether it uses AI nor what its intended purpose is.

**3. Determine role and possible risk class.** Per system: prohibited practice under Article 5, high-risk under Article 6 with Annex I or III, transparency case under Article 50, or none, each with exceptions and application dates.

**4. Collect evidence and assess gaps.** Provider information, contracts, instructions for use, data flows, oversight, logs, security and the duties of the use case. Article 26 reaches only deployers of high-risk systems; Article 50 only the cases it lists.

**5. Prioritise measures.** Every evidenced gap gets an owner, a deadline, a dependency and a verification criterion. The review cadence follows risk, change and legal developments.

sections.title: An inventory with traceable fields
sections.content:
The AI Act prescribes no spreadsheet format for deployers. Take a tool that keeps responsibilities, access rights and changes manageable.

**Useful fields:** system ID, name, version, provider, function actually used, intended and internal purpose, user groups, affected persons, data categories, integrations, your role, possible risk category with a rationale, relevant duties, approval status, responsible person, contractual and provider evidence, human oversight, logging, security controls, DPIA or FRIA status where applicable, incidents, last review, next trigger.

Reconcile the inventory with the step 1 sources and your DPIAs. Versioning and change history are good controls; whether the law requires them follows from the role and the duty. A spreadsheet alone is not evidence of compliance.

sections.title: Review questions that produce evidence
sections.content:
- **Which generative services are actually running?** Their users need Article 4 measures; check per service whether an Article 50 case applies.
- **Which HR function is active?** A system that reviews, filters or evaluates job applications may fall within Annex III, point 4(a). A brand name and an AI claim do not decide the classification.
- **Is there use outside approved accounts?** Check with lawful, proportionate sources and a secure reporting route.
- **Does a high-risk system generate logs under the deployer's control?** Article 26(6) governs their retention.
- **Are current provider information and the instructions for use available?** Request, review and version what is actually supplied.

quiz.questionText: An organisation uses AI intended to review and filter job applications. Which classification must it assess?

answerOptions.text: Minimal risk, with no obligations
Limited risk, with only a transparency duty under Article 50
High-risk under Annex III, point 4(a)
Prohibited under Article 5

quiz.explanation: Annex III, point 4(a), names AI that analyses and filters job applications. The final classification rests on the specific purpose and Article 6, including any exception under Article 6(3).

quiz.questionText: For how long must a deployer retain automatically generated logs of a high-risk AI system?

answerOptions.text: At least 30 days
At least three months
At least six months
Indefinitely, for as long as the system operates

quiz.explanation: Article 26(6): for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, at least six months, unless Union or national law provides otherwise.

quiz.questionText: What is true of the Article 30 GDPR record of processing activities as an AI inventory source?

answerOptions.text: It automatically lists every AI system, even without personal data
A useful start, to supplement with technical, contractual and organisational sources
It removes the need to review IT assets, procurement and business units
It already proves the correct AI Act risk class

quiz.explanation: The record shows only processing of personal data. It captures neither every AI system nor active functions or shadow AI, and replaces no inventory of systems, procurement and business units.

lessons.title: Connecting the GDPR, ISO 42001, and ISO 23894
lessons.subtitle: What you already have, and what is genuinely new

sections.title: Using a DPIA as a starting point
sections.content:
A DPIA under Article 35 GDPR replaces no AI Act duty; it makes information reusable. Article 26(9) requires deployers of high-risk systems to use the provider's Article 13 information for a DPIA where one is required. The overlap depends on the system, the data and the documentation; fixed coverage percentages are not reliable.

**Assess separately:**
- **GDPR:** legal basis, purpose limitation, data minimisation, data-subject rights, processing on behalf of a controller, transfers, security, Article 35.
- **Deployer obligations under Article 26:** instructions for use, human oversight, input data and logs where controlled, monitoring, information for employees and further duties by use case.
- **Provider obligations:** such as the conformity assessment and the EU declaration of conformity, which a deployer does not issue merely by using the system.
- **Article 4:** context-appropriate measures to support AI literacy, with no prescribed training plan or attestation.

Deployers within Article 27 may conduct a FRIA together with a DPIA, provided both subject matters are covered (Article 27(4)).

sections.title: ISO 42001 and ISO 23894 as structural aids
sections.content:
**ISO/IEC 42001:2023** can structure a management system for roles, objectives, risks, controls, monitoring and improvement, and **ISO/IEC 23894:2023** AI risk management. Whether individual provisions fit your role and system has to be assessed on the merits.

Certification to ISO/IEC 42001 creates no presumption of conformity under the AI Act. The presumption under Article 40 attaches to harmonised standards whose references are published in the Official Journal of the European Union; drafts and procedural status change. Map every control to the legal role and duty.

sections.title: Crosswalk: what is additional
sections.content:
A crosswalk puts common ground and differences side by side and so saves duplicate work.

- A data-processing agreement under Article 28 GDPR applies only to processing on behalf of a controller; procurement and AI Act assurances are assessed separately by role and system.
- Documentation of technical and organisational measures can reuse security controls. Article 15 addresses providers of high-risk systems; deployers have their own Article 26 and data-protection duties.
- Information under Articles 13 and 14 GDPR and under Article 26(11) of the AI Act has different conditions and content.
- The data protection officer may be involved. The AI Act does not require an “AI officer”; you settle responsibility, independence and conflicts of interest yourself.

**Additional review fields:** deployer logs (Article 26(6)), employee information (paragraph 7), EU database duties by role, Article 4 measures, response to risks and incidents (Article 26(5)), Article 22 GDPR for automated decisions.

quiz.questionText: Which standard is being prepared as the harmonised European standard for the Article 17 quality-management system?

answerOptions.text: prEN 18286

quiz.explanation: prEN 18286 is to become the harmonised standard for the Article 17 quality-management system. ISO 42001 has no Annex ZA and gives no presumption of conformity.

quiz.questionText: Your CV-screening system already has a DPIA under Article 35 GDPR. Does it replace the Article 26 AI Act duties?

answerOptions.text: Yes. The DPIA covers every AI Act obligation
No. It can support the analysis; deployer and provider duties stay separate
No. A DPIA is unrelated to the AI Act
Only a DPIA older than 24 months must be supplemented

quiz.explanation: A DPIA supplies reusable information but no fixed coverage ratio. Deployer and provider duties, such as the conformity assessment, are allocated separately.

quiz.questionText: Which article of the AI Act expressly refers to a DPIA under Article 35 GDPR?

answerOptions.text: Article 13(3)
Article 26(9)
Article 27(1)
Article 35(2)

quiz.explanation: Under Article 26(9), deployers use the Article 13 information for a required DPIA under Article 35 GDPR. No DPIA duty for every AI use follows.

lessons.title: Templates and checklists
lessons.subtitle: How to classify and maintain working templates

sections.title: A governance package ordered by priority
sections.content:
Build the eight documents of the governance package in this order: the AI acceptable-use policy, risk classification, the Article 4 training framework, the DPIA worksheet, provider due diligence, the AI inventory, the pilot charter and last the use-case assessment matrix.

These documents are implementation tools, not statutory forms, and none of them proves compliance. A DPIA is mandatory only where the conditions in Article 35 GDPR are met; risk class and deployer duties follow from the system and the role.

Build every document as a working structure: bring in the subject-matter roles, substantiate claims, record reasons for decisions, check the current law, adapt it to the use case.
sections.keyTakeaway: The eight documents are working structures; none is a statutory form or proves compliance.

sections.title: What working templates may contain
sections.content:
**AI acceptable-use policy:** scope, permitted and excluded use cases, data classes, approval routes, human review, rights, incidents, contacts, change process. The AI Act does not require a file of that name.

**Article 4 working framework:** record role, prior knowledge, context of use, affected persons and risks, and derive learning, instruction and control measures from them. The Commission names no mandatory format, no minimum hours and no mandatory attestation.

**Procurement and contract checklist:** provider information under Article 13, purpose, system version, performance limits, updates, logs, security, support, incidents, data processing, exit, evidence. Audit rights, contractual penalties, reporting cycles or a German-language requirement are negotiation points.

**Incident-response worksheet:** where there is reason to consider a risk, or on a serious incident, Article 26(5) governs notification and suspension by the deployer; the reporting duty and periods for providers sit in Article 73. Authority and reporting route depend on the implementation and the sector.

sections.title: Storage and maintenance responsibilities
sections.content:
**Storage:** a controlled system with clear owners, appropriate access rights, versioning, retention and recovery, such as Git or SharePoint; the AI Act prescribes neither.

**Maintenance:** name a responsible function. Review on changes to the system, purpose, provider, model or data, after incidents and legal changes, plus a risk-appropriate interval. The AI Act sets no fixed review interval.

**Sources:**
- EUR-Lex and the European Commission for the text of the Regulation, its timeline, guidance and AI-literacy questions and answers
- data-protection supervisory authorities for GDPR guidance
- the competent national and sectoral authorities for current enforcement and reporting information

quiz.questionText: What is the legal status of internally created working templates for governance records?

answerOptions.text: Adaptable tools with no prescribed format; duties assessed per system and role
Four documents are always mandatory and four are always voluntary
All eight documents are prescribed EU forms
Completing all eight documents automatically proves compliance

quiz.explanation: Nobody prescribes a filename or format. Whether a duty such as a DPIA applies depends on its own statutory conditions.

quiz.questionText: How often should governance records be reviewed according to this lesson?

answerOptions.text: On changes and incidents, plus a risk-based interval
Exactly once per quarter, as required by law
Only during an authority inspection
Never, once the records have been created

quiz.explanation: The AI Act prescribes no fixed review frequency. Triggers are changes to the system, purpose, provider, model or data, incidents and legal changes, plus a risk-appropriate interval.

quiz.questionText: What applies under Article 73 to a serious incident resulting in death?

answerOptions.text: Providers report within two days
Providers report immediately, within 10 days of awareness at the latest
Providers report within 15 days
Providers report within 72 hours

quiz.explanation: After a death, providers report immediately once the causal link is established or reasonably likely, within 10 days of awareness at the latest. Deployers have their own duties under Article 26(5).

lessons.title: Case study: an SME introduces a CV-screening tool
lessons.subtitle: A decision path through the Regulation
keyConcepts: section 87 of the German Works Constitution Act
three separate issues under the German General Equal Treatment Act

sections.title: Classification and duties under Article 26
sections.content:
**Fictional facts:** XY GmbH, a machinery manufacturer in Bavaria with 200 employees, buys a CV-screening system that ranks CVs by a match score and prepares a shortlist. Product and function are invented.

**Step 1, Article 5:** the purpose is none of the practices prohibited there; the specific implementation still has to be assessed.

**Step 2, Article 6 and Annex III:** point 4(a) covers AI for recruitment or selection, in particular to analyse and filter job applications. The use case falls within it unless an exception under Article 6(3) applies.

**Roles and timeline:** XY GmbH is the deployer, and the supplier stays the provider as long as no change of role under Article 25 occurs. For standalone Annex III systems, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, applicable since 27 July 2026, applies the high-risk rules from **2 December 2027**.

**Deployer obligations under Article 26 from that date:**
- Paragraph 1: use in accordance with the instructions, with technical and organisational measures.
- Paragraphs 2 and 3: human oversight by competent, trained persons with authority and support; watch automation bias.
- Paragraph 4: input data the deployer controls must be relevant and sufficiently representative for the purpose.
- Paragraph 5: monitor operation; where there is reason to consider a risk, or on a serious incident, inform the provider or distributor and the market-surveillance authority and suspend use.
- Paragraph 6: retain automatically generated logs under the deployer's control for at least six months, unless applicable law provides otherwise.
- Paragraph 7: before workplace use, inform workers' representatives and the affected workers.
- Paragraph 9: use provider information for a DPIA, which Article 35 GDPR requires where a high risk is likely; not every HR system needs one.
- Paragraph 11: inform affected persons when the system makes or assists in decisions about them.

sections.title: FRIA, roles and parallel law
sections.content:
**FRIA:** Article 27(1) covers bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services and deployers of specified systems under Annex III, point 5(b) and (c). Employment AI under Annex III, point 4, is not among them. A private machinery manufacturer using the system only for its own recruitment therefore needs no FRIA under Article 27 alone.

**Keep provider and deployer apart:**
- The conformity assessment (Article 43) and the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47) sit with the provider, as long as no change of role under Article 25 shifts duties. The deployer checks documentation, marking and the instructions for use.
- Providers of Annex III high-risk systems register under Article 49. Article 26(8) also requires deployers that are Union authorities, institutions or bodies to register; private deployers do not.

**Parallel law:**
- **Section 87(1), point 6, of the Works Constitution Act (BetrVG):** co-determination can apply where its conditions are met and a works council exists.
- **General Equal Treatment Act (AGG):** discrimination can trigger claims under section 15 and the evidential rule in section 22; amount and limits depend on the facts.
- **Article 22 GDPR:** assess whether a decision based solely on automated processing produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects a person, whether an exception applies and which safeguards are required. A merely formal human step does not reliably remove the solely automated character.

sections.title: Procurement review fields for the fictional system

quiz.questionText: A machinery manufacturer with 200 employees introduces a CV-screening system with AI ranking. Does it need a FRIA under Article 27?

answerOptions.text: Yes. Every deployment of high-risk AI triggers a FRIA
No. HR AI under Annex III, point 4, is outside Article 27
Yes, because HR AI affects fundamental rights
No, because a DPIA replaces the FRIA completely

quiz.explanation: Article 27(1) covers public bodies, private providers of public services and Annex III, point 5(b) or (c), but not a private employer merely because of HR AI under Annex III, point 4. A DPIA is assessed separately under Article 35 GDPR.

quiz.questionText: Which Article 26 duty applies specifically to an employer before a high-risk AI system is used at work?

answerOptions.text: Article 26(2): human oversight
Article 26(6): keeping logs for six months
Article 26(7): informing workers' representatives and affected workers
Article 26(11): informing applicants

quiz.explanation: Under Article 26(7), employers inform workers' representatives and affected workers before use. This is independent of co-determination under the Works Constitution Act.

quiz.questionText: Which areas of law require separate assessment for the fictional AI applicant-screening use case?

answerOptions.text: Only the EU AI Act; it displaces all other law
The AI Act, GDPR (Articles 22, 35), AGG and co-determination where applicable
The AI Act and GDPR; the AGG does not apply to AI
Only the GDPR and BetrVG; the AI Act only applies from 2027

quiz.explanation: The AI Act, the GDPR, the AGG and the Works Constitution Act can apply side by side, each with its own conditions and consequences. None follows from the label “AI” alone.
